title: Loss functions: why fitting is really optimising
intro: Much of machine learning revolves around one thing: minimising a loss. Once you understand this perspective you see connections between models, pick up new models faster and can tune them to your own problem.

blocks.html:
A loss function is a penalty score that indicates how badly the model is doing on the training data. Fitting can be seen as: shuffling the coefficients (parameters) until that penalty score is as small as possible. Least squares linear regression (like LinearRegression) minimises the sum of the squared errors on the training set, with the error defined as the difference between the true and the predicted target.

Note a subtle but important distinction: the loss is used to fit the model; the score is used to see how it is going. Often they coincide, but that is not guaranteed.

blocks.label: squared loss (linear regression)
blocks.caption: Least squares: the sum of squared errors over all training examples.

rows: "which parameters make the error on the training data small?"
"how well does the model perform on (new) data?"

blocks.html:
For classification the squared error is unsuitable, because y values are categories, not numbers. The most natural candidate: count your mistakes. That is the 0-1 loss — per example it is 0 (prediction correct) or 1 (prediction wrong), and the sum over the training set is exactly the number of mistakes made.

Conceptually neat, but in practice this loss is very hard to minimise directly — which is why logistic regression and SVMs do not use it. They adopt a smooth (differentiable) approximation that can be optimised efficiently.

blocks.label: 0-1 loss
blocks.caption: The sum over all training examples = the number of mistakes on the training set.

blocks.html:
What does that minimisation look like? With scipy.optimize.minimize you can optimise arbitrary functions. Minimise \( y = x^2 \) from a starting point and the algorithms find a value very close to zero — typically something like \( 10^{-8} \). That is normal in numerical optimisation: you rarely get the exact answer, but something very close to it.

As a concrete example, you can minimise the squared error of linear regression, with the coefficients as inputs. The code then literally answers the question: "which values of the coefficients make my squared error as small as possible?" — which is exactly what linear regression does.

blocks.caption: scipy.optimize.minimize in action
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

# Minimise y = x^2, starting from x = 3
result = minimize(np.square, x0=3.0)
print('minimum at x =', result.x[0])
print('loss value    =', result.fun)

# And from a different starting point
result2 = minimize(np.square, x0=-10.0)
print('from -10      :', result2.x[0])

blocks.html: Don't expect exact zeros: numerical optimisation gives answers "in the neighbourhood" — \( \approx 10^{-8} \) is a perfectly fine result.
